label: Design effective escalation and ambiguity resolution patterns
model: claude-opus-5 (authored in a Claude Code session)

cards.front: Why is getting escalation wrong costly in BOTH directions?
cards.back: Under-escalating causes harm; over-escalating destroys the value of the automation. The fix is escalation built on explicit, deterministic rules rather than vague heuristics or fluctuating model confidence scores.

cards.front: What separates a good escalation trigger from a bad one? Give an example of each.
cards.back: A good trigger is measurable, testable and improvable — 'escalate when intent confidence falls below 0.7 after two clarification turns'. A bad one is untestable and drifts — 'escalate when the agent feels unsure'. Triggers should be structured conditions evaluated at decision points in the loop, each producing a typed escalation event.

cards.front: Name the three categories that reliably warrant escalation.
cards.back: 1) Confidence thresholds — ambiguity unresolved after a bounded number of clarification attempts; stop rather than guess. 2) Policy violations — refunds above a threshold, account closures, legal complaints, protected personal data: rules, not judgments. 3) Sensitive topics — crisis language, self-harm, vulnerability, regulated medical/legal/financial advice, where the agent's job is to detect and route, not respond substantively.

cards.front: Give the three reasons sentiment analysis is a poor primary escalation trigger.
cards.back: 1) Noisy signal — frustration in language doesn't reliably map to needing a human; many frustrated customers are satisfied by a correct automated resolution. 2) Latency mismatch — sentiment scores past utterances, but the escalation decision must anticipate the next moment. 3) Adversarial brittleness — users who learn the system escalates on frustration will feign it to bypass automation.

cards.front: If not sentiment, what should escalation be based on?
cards.back: Escalate on WHAT HAPPENED — a policy threshold crossed, a failed resolution attempt, an explicit request — not on HOW IT SOUNDED. Sentiment may be used as a soft modifier at most, never as a primary trigger.

cards.front: What must an escalation hand off besides control?
cards.back: Context. The minimal payload is the reason (which trigger fired), a conversation summary, the urgency level, and the customer's stated goal — plus attempts made and a timestamp. Handing off only a customer ID forces the human to re-read everything from scratch.

cards.front: Exam trap: is a single global confidence threshold acceptable?
cards.back: No — define thresholds PER DOMAIN or task type. A 0.7 threshold may suit order tracking but is far too permissive for a billing dispute, which tolerates much less uncertainty than a product FAQ.

cards.front: How do customer preferences fit into the escalation decision?
cards.back: As a first-class input, not an afterthought. A preference record specifies the preferred channel (chat/callback/email), escalation sensitivity (low/normal/high), and explicit opt-outs or always-escalate topics. Overriding a stated 'I want a human for this' damages trust even when the automated answer is technically correct.

cards.front: In what order should a deterministic shouldEscalate() evaluate its checks?
cards.back: Customer-preference always-escalate topics → sensitive topics → policy thresholds (e.g. refund > $500) → low confidence (< 0.7 AND clarification attempts ≥ 2). It returns a typed trigger or null, so the decision is testable.

cards.front: Exam trap: should an agent treat escalation as a failure to avoid?
cards.back: No — escalation is a DESIGNED OUTCOME, not an exception. Agents that hide escalations or retry indefinitely to avoid them cause more harm than agents that escalate cleanly and early.
